opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated constraints, actually. A lot of the discussion about AI timelines focuses on algorithms, or on how much money people are willing to spend, but at some point you run into the fact that you need to physically build things: fabs, data centers, power plants, transmission lines. Those operate on timescales that are much slower than the timescales people imagine when they talk about very rapid AI progress.

If you look at the trend, training compute for frontier models has been growing about four to five times per year. Part of that has been absorbed by existing slack. There was spare capacity in the chip supply chain, and companies could reallocate GPUs that were being used for other things. But that slack runs out. If you want to keep scaling at that rate for another several years, you're eventually talking about training runs that need gigawatts of power, and that requires new generation capacity and new grid connections. In the US, getting a large power plant built and interconnected can take many years, partly because of permitting and regulatory delays, not just the physical construction.

Semiconductors are similar. A new leading-edge fab takes something like three to five years to go from decision to volume production, and it costs tens of billions of dollars. So if demand for AI chips suddenly jumps, supply can't respond immediately. You have a lag there that's on the order of years.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. These constraints slow scaling down, but they don't stop it. When there's enough economic value at stake, people find ways around bottlenecks. You can build gas turbines on-site instead of waiting for grid connections, you can distribute training across multiple data centers, you can pay premiums to accelerate construction. And if AI systems themselves start contributing to the economy in a big way, the amount of capital available for this buildout grows a lot.

So my view is that physical infrastructure is a big part of why I expect the transition to be more gradual than some people think. It's not going to be a situation where one lab has a breakthrough and then a month later everything is transformed. The world has a certain inertia, and building physical capital is a large part of that inertia. But over a span of a decade or two, I think these constraints can be overcome, and the economy could end up growing much faster than it does today.

r001.rationale: The response says premiums can accelerate construction, but does not say increased spending yields only a small reduction in construction time.

r002.rationale: It describes power and fab build times as year-scale bottlenecks and says physical infrastructure is a major reason the transition will be more gradual, connecting construction delays to AI scaling pace.

r003.rationale: It says AI-driven economic value could increase capital available for infrastructure, but does not state that rapid economic-output growth is required for that feedback loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most underrated constraints, and it's the one I find myself pointing to most often when people ask me why I don't expect the kind of extremely fast takeoff scenarios that some people talk about.

The basic picture is that AI scaling right now runs on a few physical inputs: chips, data centers to put them in, and electricity to power them. And all three of those have fairly long lead times. If you want to build a new fab, you're talking about something like three to five years from the decision to actually producing chips at volume. Data centers are faster, but once you get to the gigawatt scale that the frontier labs are now planning for, you run into power. And power is the slow one. Building new generation capacity, getting grid interconnections, transmission lines, permitting—in the US a lot of that is measured in years, sometimes closer to a decade for transmission. So even if you had unlimited capital and unlimited demand, there's a question of how fast the physical world lets you turn that money into compute.

Now, I want to be careful here, because historically compute has grown at something like four or five x per year for the frontier training runs, and so far the physical constraints haven't actually been binding. Hardware improvements, better chips per dollar, plus just spending more money has carried most of that. But the reason it hasn't been binding is that AI was a small fraction of global semiconductor output and a small fraction of electricity consumption. Once you're at the point where AI is, say, a few percent of US electricity and is the dominant customer for leading-edge fabs, you can't keep growing at that rate just by taking share from other uses. You have to actually expand the pie, and expanding the pie is where the lead times bite.

So my rough expectation is that compute growth slows down somewhat from the current pace over the next several years, not because people stop wanting to spend, but because the supply chain can't accommodate five x per year indefinitely. Maybe you get something more like two to three x per year once you're genuinely infrastructure-limited. That's still extremely fast by the standards of any other industry. It's just slower than the extrapolation people sometimes do.

The other thing I'd say is that this interacts with the question of how much AI can accelerate its own development. A lot of the fast takeoff arguments implicitly assume that the bottleneck is cognitive labor—algorithms, research, engineering—and that once AI can do that, you get this very rapid loop. But if a large share of progress comes from compute scaling, and compute scaling is bottlenecked on things like pouring concrete and building transformers and getting permits, then having very smart AI researchers helps less than you'd think. The AI can't will a power plant into existence faster. It can make the chip designs better, it can improve the algorithms, and that matters, but there's a floor on how long the physical stuff takes that intelligence doesn't straightforwardly remove.

I'd actually push back a little on people who take that too far in the other direction, though. Humans have historically been pretty slow at building infrastructure partly because of coordination and regulatory reasons, not purely physical ones. China builds power plants much faster than the US does. So some of the "it takes ten years" is a policy choice rather than a law of physics, and if the economic stakes get high enough, I'd expect some of that to compress. But even in the compressed case you're looking at years, not months, and that's enough to rule out the most extreme scenarios where everything happens in a single year.

r001.rationale: It says unlimited capital cannot overcome long physical lead times and that policy changes could compress them, but does not state that more infrastructure spending would yield only a small reduction in construction time.

r002.rationale: It explains that compute growth could slow because fabs, power generation, grid connections, and transmission take years to build, making physical infrastructure a constraint on AI scaling.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss economic output needing to grow rapidly for a feedback loop from output to further AI scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think it could be a pretty important constraint, because there’s a difference between being willing to spend money on compute and actually being able to get that compute online. You need chips, data centers, power, and the infrastructure connecting all of those things. And those have different lead times.

If you suddenly decide you want to build a much larger training cluster, you can’t necessarily accelerate every part of that process just by spending more money. Expanding semiconductor manufacturing capacity takes time. Building power generation and transmission takes time. Even if you have the chips, you might not have a site where you can supply enough electricity to run them.

The important question, though, is how much of that demand people anticipate. If companies expect scaling to continue, they can start building infrastructure years before they need it. So a long construction time doesn’t automatically imply slow growth. It does mean that an unexpected increase in demand is harder to accommodate. If AI suddenly becomes much more economically valuable, spending could rise much faster than the physical capacity available to absorb it.

And I’d distinguish scaling physical compute from improving AI capabilities. Better algorithms and more efficient use of existing hardware can still produce progress while infrastructure catches up. So I’d expect these constraints to limit how quickly the physical side can expand, rather than impose a fixed speed limit on AI progress overall.

r001.rationale: It says spending more cannot necessarily accelerate every infrastructure step, but does not state that spending yields only a small reduction in construction time.

r002.rationale: It says infrastructure constraints limit physical compute expansion, but does not state that serial construction times determine the overall pace of AI scaling.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss a feedback loop from economic output to further AI scaling or require rapid economic-output growth for that loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could become a fairly important constraint, because the time it takes to build infrastructure doesn’t necessarily shrink as quickly as the time it takes to improve AI. You can have a better algorithm and deploy it on hardware you already own, but if you want substantially more compute, you need chips, data centers, and electricity. Those things have construction timelines, and spending more money only helps so much.

Power is a particularly interesting case. It’s not just whether there’s enough electricity in aggregate; it’s whether you can get enough power at a particular location, with the connections and equipment you need. You might be able to build the data center faster than you can arrange its power supply.

On the other hand, infrastructure can be built in anticipation of demand. If companies expect AI to be enormously valuable, they can start projects well before they need the capacity. So the constraint depends partly on how surprising the growth is. A sudden jump in demand is much harder to accommodate than growth people have been planning for.

And I would distinguish scaling physical compute from scaling capabilities. Infrastructure could put a ceiling on how quickly the amount of compute grows, while algorithmic improvements still allow capabilities to advance quite rapidly. So I’d expect it to introduce delays and bottlenecks, but I wouldn’t assume that translates into a similarly slow pace of AI progress overall.

r001.rationale: “Spending more money only helps so much” conveys that increased spending may reduce construction time only to a limited extent.

r002.rationale: The response says infrastructure can constrain compute growth, but distinguishes that from the overall pace of AI progress and does not say infrastructure timelines could determine AI scaling overall.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that an economic-output feedback loop requires output to grow rapidly.
